newsitem.title: USA: Tighter US beef, more pork supplies ahead - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Tighter US beef, more pork supplies ahead - analyst.

text.p: Less beef but more pork will likely grace U.S. supermarket coolers late in 1997, said Chuck Alaron, senior livestock analyst with Alaron Trading Corp.

In remarks delivered to livestock producers Tuesday in Dodge City, Kan., Levitt, who is based in Chicago, said pork prices could peak when cattle prices are at their lows early in the year, and vice versa later in 1997.
Beef production, partly from herd liquidation, will ease into 1997 while stepped up pork production will develop from an aggressive expansion of hog breeding herds, Levitt said.

Cow-calf producers have begun to aggressively liquidate a herd that they had just spent the better part of six years building up and by the start of 1998 the U.S. breeding herd is likely to be close to the 1991 level, Levitt said. Feeder cattle supplies will be tightening considerably by the second half of 1997, feeling the impact of a reduced calf crop and making fed beef output levels difficult to sustain by late next year, he added.
Hog prices are expected to advance from now into spring and perhaps reach their 1997 peak at that time, rather than in the summer which is normal seasonally.
"We would not be surprised to see market hog prices in Iowa very close to Kansas choice steer prices on a per hundred weight basis at that time," he said.

But, as 1997 progresses, downward pressure on hog prices is likely to mount. By late spring, year over year increases in production should begin and by next fall a five percent increase is possible, he said.
"By next fall (hog prices) could be as much as $15.00 to $20.00 per hundred weight below those seen in the spring," Levitt added.
